pr_title: fix(ivy): unable to bind to properties that start with class or style
pr_body:
Fixes Ivy picking up property bindings that start with `class` or `style` as if they're style bindings.

Fixes #32310.

issue_context.title: [ivy] If an @Input *begins* with the word 'class' it is treated as a CSS class
issue_context.body:
# 🐞 bug report ### Affected Package It's an Ivy bug, I don't know exactly which package ### Is this a regression? Yes, it only happens with Ivy turned on. Reproduced on 8.2.3 ### Description With Ivy turned on, if a component has an @ Input that begins with the word 'class', e.g. ```@Input() classesInMySchool: any[]``` it is treated as a CSS class instead of a regular property and it is not included in the list of inputs. Any code using this property doesn't work - the value is `undefined`. The compiled form looks like ``` const ctx_r18467 = _angular_core__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_0__["ɵɵnextContext"](); _angular_core__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_0__["ɵɵclassMap"](ctx_r18467.classes); _angular_core__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_0__["ɵɵstylingApply"](); ``` It appears to be based on the name of the input rather than the name of the class property in the event that they are different. ## 🔬 Minimal Reproduction Minimal reproduction here: https://github.com/llimos/angular-class-prefix-bug Steps to reproduce: 1. Either build or ng serve with Ivy turned on 2. See that the 'classesInMySchool' property didn't make it through to the child component, so 'it didn't work' is displayed 3. Switch off ivy in tsconfig.app.json 4. Repeat step 2 and see that it works normally - 'child works' is displayed ## 🔥 Exception or Error None ## 🌍 Your Environment **Angular Version:** 

Angular CLI: 8.3.0
Node: 10.15.1
OS: win32 x64
Angular: 8.2.3

**Anything else relevant?** We are working on educational software for schools, so as you can imagine there are rather a lot of properties beginning with the word 'class' and changing them all as a workaround is unfeasible.

review_comments: Why not use a regular expression?
I wanted it to be explicit what we support. Also we'd need at least two regular expressions to also handle class bindings.

FWIW, you can do it with one RegExp, but it is not going to be super readable and I suspect it would be slower too (not necessarily noticeably so, but still). E.g.:

```js
const [, isClass, isStyle] = /^(?:(class)(?:Name$)?|(style))(?:[.!]|$)/.exec(name);
```
@crisbeto use a regex and add a series of comments explaining why and when each case is used.
Honestly, I'd prefer just doing the readable way. I don't really see a benefit in obscuring it with a regex since it's not faster.
Agreed that the explicit string checking is preferable
